title: Temperature and kinetic theory
lede: Temperature is average molecular kinetic energy, heat is energy in transit, and the ideal gas law ties the two pictures together.

cards.heading: Absolute temperature
cards.body: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of a substance's molecules; absolute zero (0 K = -273 C) is the floor where that motion is minimal. Kelvin and Celsius degrees are the same size, so T(K) = T(C) + 273. Only absolute temperature may be multiplied or divided in gas formulas — ratios of Celsius readings are meaningless.

cards.heading: Gas law and speed
cards.body: The ideal gas law PV = nRT links pressure, volume, moles, and absolute temperature, with R = 8.31 J/(mol K). Kinetic theory goes further: the rms molecular speed is v = sqrt(3RT/M), where M is molar mass in kilograms per mole. Hotter means faster, heavier means slower — nitrogen at room temperature averages roughly 500 m/s.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: How much heat raises 0.40 kg of aluminum from 25 C to 55 C? Aluminum's specific heat is 900 J/(kg K), so Q = mc*delta-T = (0.40)(900)(30) = 10,800 J. The same 10,800 J poured into 0.40 kg of water (c = 4186) would warm it only about 6.5 C, showing how much more energy water soaks up per degree.

flashcards.explain: Pressure times volume equals moles times R times absolute temperature, with R = 8.31 J/(mol K). Always convert temperature to kelvin and pressure to pascals before plugging in.

Speed grows with the square root of absolute temperature and shrinks with the square root of molar mass in kg/mol. This is why light gases like helium zip around faster than heavy ones at the same temperature.

flashcards.meaning: Heat needed for a temperature change
flashcards.explain: Mass times specific heat times temperature change. Specific heat is the energy per kilogram per kelvin, and water's 4186 J/(kg K) is unusually large among everyday substances.

mcq.prompt: 1.5 mol of an ideal gas sits at 400 K and a pressure of 200 kPa. What volume does it occupy?
mcq.wrongExplain: 0.050 m^3 halves the pressure to 100 kPa, 0.0125 m^3 uses 200 K instead of 400 K, and 2.5 m^3 forgets to convert kPa into pascals.

title: First law and PV work
lede: A gas's energy changes only through heat flowing in and work being done — a checking account with exactly two transaction types.

cards.heading: The first law
cards.body: The internal energy of a system changes by delta-U = Q - W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done by the system. Both signs matter: heat leaving or work done on the gas are negative entries. This is energy conservation with heat included.

cards.heading: Work and processes
cards.body: At constant pressure, an expanding gas does work W = P*delta-V. Isothermal: temperature pinned, so for an ideal gas delta-U = 0 and Q = W. Adiabatic: no heat exchanged, Q = 0, so delta-U = -W. Isobaric keeps the pressure fixed; isochoric keeps the volume fixed, so no work is done.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: A gas at constant pressure 1.0e5 Pa expands by 2.0e-3 m^3 (2.0 liters) while absorbing 600 J of heat. The work done by the gas is W = (1.0e5)(2.0e-3) = 200 J, so the internal energy rises by delta-U = 600 - 200 = 400 J. The other 200 J of heat paid for pushing the piston.

flashcards.meaning: First law, with work done BY the gas positive
flashcards.explain: Heat added and work output are both positive entries here. Some texts flip the work sign, so check the convention before plugging in; the physics is the same either way.
On a PV diagram, work is the area under the curve. At constant pressure that area is just height times width: pressure times the volume swept out by the piston.
With Q = 0 the first law gives delta-U = -W, so an adiabatic expansion cools the gas and compression warms it. Fast processes are roughly adiabatic because heat flow takes time.

mcq.prompt: An ideal gas expands isothermally and does 150 J of work on its surroundings. How much heat flows into the gas?
mcq.rightExplain: Isothermal means delta-U = 0 for an ideal gas, so Q = W = 150 J: all the work is paid for by heat flowing in.
mcq.wrongExplain: 0 J confuses this with a free expansion where no work is done, -150 J flips the sign convention, and 300 J adds Q and W instead of balancing them.

title: Heat engines and entropy
lede: Heat never flows uphill for free: every engine pays a tax to the cold reservoir, and entropy is the tax collector.

cards.heading: Heat engines
cards.body: An engine takes heat Qh from a hot reservoir, converts some to work W, and dumps the rest Qc into a cold reservoir. Its efficiency is e = W/Qh = 1 - Qc/Qh. Carnot's theorem caps this at e = 1 - Tc/Th using absolute temperatures — no engine can beat a reversible one running between the same two reservoirs.

cards.heading: Refrigerators and entropy
cards.body: A refrigerator runs the flow backwards: work input moves heat from the cold box into the warm room. Entropy change is delta-S = Q/T for heat Q entering at temperature T, and the second law says the universe's total entropy never decreases. That single inequality is why perfectly efficient engines and perpetual motion machines are impossible.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: An engine runs between a boiler at 500 K and the environment at 300 K. The Carnot bound is e = 1 - 300/500 = 0.40, so at best 40 percent of the absorbed heat becomes work. If the engine takes in 1000 J per cycle, the maximum work is 400 J and at least 600 J must be exhausted as waste heat.

flashcards.explain: Kelvin only: reservoirs at 227 C and 27 C mean 500 K and 300 K, giving 40 percent, not 88. Every real engine falls short of this bound because of friction and unrestrained heat flow.

The same joule of heat adds more entropy to a cold reservoir than to a hot one, because T is in the denominator. That asymmetry is exactly why heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold and never the reverse.

flashcards.meaning: Second law: total entropy never decreases
flashcards.explain: A local entropy drop is allowed only if something nearby gains more. This is the physical arrow of time, and it is the reason no cyclic device can turn heat entirely into work.

mcq.prompt: An inventor claims an engine whose hot reservoir is at 227 C and whose cold reservoir is at 27 C. What is the maximum possible efficiency?
mcq.rightExplain: Convert first: 227 C = 500 K and 27 C = 300 K, so e = 1 - 300/500 = 0.40, or 40 percent.
mcq.wrongExplain: 88 percent is what you get plugging the Celsius readings straight into the formula, 60 percent is the heat fraction that must be rejected (Tc/Th), and 100 percent would require a cold reservoir at absolute zero.
